---
title: "Converting a deposit"
---

```{r}
#| label: queue
library(data.table)
q <- as.data.table(read.csv("../queue/candidates.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
# Statuses carry a reason after a colon ("held: no licence", "available: survey
# evidence unverified"), so classify on the word before it.
q[, state := fifelse(grepl("^built", status), "built",
             fifelse(grepl("^claimed", status), "claimed",
             fifelse(grepl("^available", status), "available",
             fifelse(grepl("^needs-look", status), "needs-look", "held"))))]
counts <- q[, .N, by = state]
n <- function(s) { v <- counts[state == s, N]; if (length(v)) v else 0L }
```

The project is at the stage where the most useful thing anyone can do is
convert another public deposit and see what breaks. There are
`r n("available")` inspected candidates waiting, `r n("needs-look")` more that
nobody has opened yet, `r n("claimed")` claimed, `r n("built")` built and
`r n("held")` held back (an access wall, no licence, or a design the standard
does not yet cover). Each conversion is one R script plus the files it writes.

## The checklist

Do these in order. Each step can stop a deposit, and the early steps are the
cheap ones.

1. **[Licence](#licence).** Check it on the source page. Some licences mean stop.
2. **[Sample floor](#sample-floor).** Count the units and the repeat surveys.
   A small table still ships, but you should know before you start.
3. **[Build and check](#build-and-check).** Write the script, run it, and check
   the table in the [browser validator](validate.qmd). The command-line validator
   runs the same checks locally.
4. **[Issue](#open-an-issue).** Open a data-queue issue, so nobody else builds the
   same deposit.
5. **[Pull request](#open-a-pull-request).** Commit the script and its records,
   not the data, and open a pull request against `main`.

Set up your computer first ([Before you start](#before-you-start)). Do it once,
and update your copy each time you begin a new deposit.

## Before you start

**Install the tools.** You need git, R (4.1 or later) and Python (3.9 or later).

```bash
# R packages, from a terminal (or run the install.packages() line inside R)
Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("data.table", "jsonlite", "readxl"), repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")'

# Python: pandas for the validator, pytest if you want to run its tests
python3 -m pip install pandas pytest
```

`readxl` is needed only for deposits that ship Excel files, but it is easiest to
install it now.

**Fork and clone.** Fork [`ben-domingue/eco`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco)
on GitHub, then clone your fork and tell git where the original lives:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/eco.git
cd eco
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco.git
```

**Update before every new deposit.** The standard and the tools change often (the
standard moved to v1.1 within days of the first outside contribution). Start each
deposit from the current `main`, on a branch named `<your-username>/<table>`:

```bash
git checkout main
git pull upstream main
git push origin main            # keeps your fork's main in step
git checkout -b <your-username>/<table>
```

Everything below runs from the top folder of the repository.

## 1. Licence {#licence}

Open the deposit's page (Dryad, Zenodo, ...) and read the licence it shows there.
Then check the deposited readme and data files for a different licence, because
the stricter of the two applies.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Licence policy (draft for Ben to confirm)

Adapted from IRW's "Before you start" and eco's intake rules
([standard, Intake policy](standard.qmd)):

- **CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA or public domain:** go ahead.
- **Non-commercial (CC BY-NC and the like), ODbL, GPL or another licence that
  carries a condition forward:** go ahead. The condition goes into the table's
  `derived_license`, so anyone who needs to can find and exclude the table.
- **No licence, a licence code that does not resolve to a named licence, or
  "contact the author":** stop. Email the owner for written permission (IRW's
  template is `processing_notes/Licensing.txt` in `ben-domingue/irw`), and build
  nothing until it arrives.
- **ND (no derivatives):** stop. Reshaping the data into eco's format is a
  derivative, which ND forbids.
- **The repository page and the files disagree** (say, Dryad shows CC0 but the
  readme says ODbL): the stricter licence applies and is carried forward. Record
  both in the dictionary row.
- **Scraped or re-uploaded third-party data:** do not host it under any licence.
  The re-uploader cannot license data they did not own.

Anything that fits none of these: ask in an issue before writing code.
:::

While you are on the page, check that nobody has the deposit already. Search
[the queue](#the-queue) and the dictionary
(`dictionary/dictionary_auto.csv`) for its DOI, and look for an open
[data-queue issue](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/issues?q=label%3A%22data+queue%22).

## 2. Sample floor {#sample-floor}

eco reports a sample floor on every table rather than rejecting small ones. A
table **meets** the floor with at least 30 units (sites, cameras, animals...) and
at least 2 repeat surveys per unit (2 periods for capture-recapture). Below that
it still ships, marked `below`, so users can filter it out, and it is a lower
priority. Count both numbers from the deposit's description before you start.
The script also reports them (`floor=meets` in its last line).

Check the design too: the [standard's scope (E9)](standard.qmd) lists which
designs are in. Presence-only records, telemetry and model outputs are out.

## 3. Build and check {#build-and-check}

**Start from the closest existing script.** `data/README.md` lists every table
built so far, with its design. Pick one with the same design and the same kind of
deposit, copy it to `data/<table>.R`, and change it. For example,
`data/samek_2024_racerunner_occ.R` is a short single-season occupancy script built
from a Dryad matrix. The repository's own instructions for agents
(`.claude/skills/eco-convert-deposit/SKILL.md`) give the order of steps and name
model scripts for several kinds of deposit.

**Write the header first.** The script is the record of how the table was made.
Its opening comment says where the data came from, the licence as shown, the
paper, what each deposited file holds, and how each column maps onto the standard.

**Decide how the survey set is evidenced.** In plain terms: how do you know that a
0 means "surveyed, not found" rather than "never surveyed"? eco keeps a row for
every survey that happened and none for surveys that did not, so the table has to
say what that list of surveys rests on. The script records one of these as
`surveyEvidence`:

| Value | Use it when the deposit has |
|---|---|
| `deposited_matrix` | a site-by-visit grid where "not surveyed" (blank or `NA`) and "not detected" (0) look different |
| `sample_table` | a list of the surveys that were carried out |
| `effort_table` | effort per site and visit; a survey happened where effort is above 0 |
| `row_presence` | one row per survey, including rows that recorded nothing |
| `inferred` | none of these; you reconstruct the surveys with a rule, and the script states the rule |

If you cannot tell surveyed from not surveyed at all, the deposit cannot be built.
Say so in an issue.

**Run it.**

```bash
Rscript data/<table>.R
```

The script downloads the deposit into `.cache/raw/<table>/` and writes the table
into `output/`. It also adds a row to `dictionary/dictionary_auto.csv` and
`tags/tags_auto.csv`. If an assertion fails, the script stops with the line that
failed. That usually means the deposit differs from what the script expects, so
fix the script, not the check.

**Check it in your browser.** Drop the files from `output/` (the core CSV, its
`__taxa.csv` and any other side tables, and `__dataset.json`) on the
[browser validator](validate.qmd). Nothing is uploaded. It answers two questions:
does the table conform to the standard, and does it pass the upload checks.

**Check it on the command line.** This runs the same checks locally:

```bash
python3 -m eco_validate.cli output/<table>.csv -v
```

It ends with an **exit code**, a number the command hands back to the terminal:
0 means it passed, and anything else means something blocks the table. Run
`echo $?` straight afterwards to see it. Errors must be fixed; warnings are worth
reading, and some are expected (an `inferred` survey set always gives one).

**Optional: the IRW check.** Every eco table must also be a valid
[IRW](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org) table, and the maintainers check that
before upload. To run it yourself, clone IRW once, anywhere, and point
`IRW_SRC` at the clone, which is the folder that contains `irw_validate/`:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ben-domingue/irw.git ~/irw
IRW_SRC=~/irw python3 -m eco_validate.cli output/<table>.csv -v --irw
```

Without `IRW_SRC`, `--irw` reports `irw_validate not importable` and fails. The
IRW validator adds warnings that are normal for ecological tables, such as
`sample_floor` (IRW's floor of 100 does not apply to animal data) and
`cov_prefix` (IRW does not know eco's `obs_` columns).

## 4. Open an issue {#open-an-issue}

[Open a data-queue issue](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/issues/new?template=data_queue.yml)
titled with your table name (`author_year_place_type`). The form asks for the
deposit, its licence, the design, the survey evidence, coordinates and taxon
sensitivity, so a maintainer can spot a problem before you finish. You can open
it before step 3 to reserve the deposit; the queue's rules are in
`queue/README.md`.

## 5. Open a pull request {#open-a-pull-request}

The tables themselves live on Redivis, not in the repository, and `output/*.csv`
is gitignored. Commit only the records of how the table was made:

| Commit | What it is |
|---|---|
| `data/<table>.R` | your script |
| `output/<table>__dataset.json` | the table's metadata and counts (the only file in `output/` that is tracked) |
| your rows in `dictionary/dictionary_auto.csv` and `tags/tags_auto.csv` | written by the script |
| your row in `metadata/metadata.csv` | made by `metadata/run_pipeline.sh 01` |
| your row in `queue/candidates.csv` | `status` set to `built: <table>`, your name in `claimed_by` |
| a row in `data/README.md` | under "Tables built so far" |

Before you push, run the checks that CI runs on every pull request:

```bash
metadata/run_pipeline.sh 01                 # adds your table's metadata.csv row
python3 tools/check_coverage.py             # every table has its dictionary, tags and metadata rows
python3 tools/check_prose_numbers.py --strict   # numbers in your titles match the table
python3 -m pytest eco_validate/tests -q     # the validator's own tests
```

Stage 01 stops if `output/` holds a core CSV without its `__dataset.json`, for
example one left over from another branch. Move that CSV aside and run it again.

Then commit, push to your fork and open a pull request against
`ben-domingue/eco:main` that names the issue (`#<number>`). Say in the
description what the checks reported and anything you were unsure of. A
maintainer reruns the script and uploads the table to Redivis, where it is
validated again before it ships. Pull requests from forks wait for a maintainer to
approve their CI run.

## How a table is built

One script per source lives in `data/`. It downloads the deposit into a local
cache, reshapes it into the standard, validates it, and writes

| Output | Where | Committed? |
|---|---|---|
| the clean long-format CSV | `output/<table>.csv` | no |
| side tables for taxa, primary periods, units and traps | `output/<table>__taxa.csv`, `__periods.csv`, `__units.csv`, `__traps.csv` | no |
| dataset metadata with the EML and Darwin Core fields, counts and sample-floor status | `output/<table>__dataset.json` | yes |
| a Data-Dictionary row and a tags row | `dictionary/dictionary_auto.csv`, `tags/tags_auto.csv` | yes |

Shared helpers (cached downloads, GBIF taxon matching, coordinate coarsening,
the writer and the staging functions) are in `lib/eco_common.R`; the
converters are the R package's `Rpkg/R/convert.R`. The writer runs an R twin of
the validator and refuses a bad table; the Python validator is the authority.

## Conventions the scripts follow

- **The script is the processing record.** Its header comment states the
  source, licence, paper, the file layout as deposited, the mapping onto the
  standard, and what was not shipped and why. There is no separate notes file.
- **Assertions, not comments, for facts about the source.** Row counts, value
  sets, that the missingness pattern is identical across species, that effort
  is positive exactly where a survey exists. A re-download that changes the
  source fails loudly.
- **Explicit zeros.** A row exists if and only if a survey happened. A blank
  cell in a deposited matrix becomes a missing row, never a missing `y`, and
  the metadata says what the survey set rests on (`surveyEvidence`).
- **Species codes on `taxon`**, short and upper case. The scientific name,
  GBIF taxon key and any traits go to the `__taxa` side table.
- **Period-level facts** (season label, calendar year) go to `__periods`, not
  into the core file.
- **Model outputs are not covariates.** A covariate the authors estimated
  from the same detections is dropped, and the drop is logged.
- **Coordinates are never finer than the source.** Taxa the source or a red
  list flags as sensitive get a 0.1-degree coarsening, with the uncertainty
  column and the dataset flag set.
- **Table names** follow the standard's intake policy:
  `author_year_taxonOrPlace_type`, lower case, 40 characters or fewer.

## The queue

The queue is `queue/candidates.csv`, seeded from the discovery pass with
deposits that have recoverable non-detections and a conversion difficulty of
1 to 4 on a 5-point scale. It stays the index of every candidate; an issue
records each claim. To claim one, open a
[data-queue issue](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/issues/new?template=data_queue.yml)
titled with the table name you intend to use, and in your pull request set the
row's status to `built: <table>` with your name in `claimed_by`. New candidates go
at the bottom with status `available`. The statuses are explained in
`queue/README.md`.

```{r}
#| label: queue-table
#| output: asis
setorder(q, state, difficulty_1to5)
out <- q[, .(Candidate = candidate, Source = source, `DOI / URL` = doi_or_url,
             Licence = license, `Data type` = data_type, Difficulty = difficulty_1to5,
             Status = status)]
cat(knitr::kable(out, format = "pipe"), sep = "\n")
```

## Where the data lives

The discovery pass found that the data exists in volume and is overwhelmingly
CC0. Dryad is the richest source by far, with on the order of a thousand
word-match hits for "detection history" and "detection/non-detection", of
which perhaps a quarter to two fifths are real detection, count or capture
data. Dryad's API refuses anonymous per-file downloads, and most deposits have
no Zenodo mirror; what Dryad does serve anonymously is the zip of a whole
deposit version, which is what `download_dryad()` in `lib/eco_common.R` fetches
and caches. Zenodo
natively adds MARK input files; USGS ScienceBase, EDI, KNB and the Dataverses
add smaller numbers of clean, well-documented series; GBIF sampling-event
datasets, NEON and the Breeding Bird Survey are each a large integration
project in their own right. The full account is in the repository's
[discovery summary](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/discovery_summary.md).
